title.title: Optimal-order randomized $k$-server on every metric
title.subtitle: Claim: a randomized online policy is $O(\log^2(k+1))$-competitive on every metric space, finite or not

plain: Taxis wait around a city while calls arrive without warning: how much extra driving does not knowing cost?

object.xlabel: number of points $n$ in the metric

beats.text: $k$ servers, requests arriving online: pay for every move, compare with hindsight
Schematically: the old bound also grew with the number of points $n$
Claimed: no dependence on $n$, matching the $\Omega(\log^2 k)$ lower bound of 2023

steps: Cut the space into nested regions at many scales
Treat the regions as a tree and spread the servers down it
Pin the spread to real points, then round to whole servers
One log comes from cutting, one from spreading

achievement.label: Randomized k-server after the 2023 lower bound
achievement.context: Before: $O(\log^2 k \log n)$ on $n$-point metrics; $\Omega(\log^2 k)$ needed on some (Bubeck–Coester–Rabani)
achievement.note: Existence only; the efficient version's additive constant 'may be enormous'

verify.ourCheck: We did not build the Lean or referee the proof

voice.text: Servers chase requests with no view of the future. How much extra movement is unavoidable?
Nested regions at every scale, servers spread down the tree, then rounded.
Claimed: log squared, on every space.

sources.quote: refuted by Bubeck-Coester-Rabani (STOC 2023, arXiv 2211.05753) with an Omega(log^2 k) lower bound
Bubeck-Cohen-Lee-Lee-Madry O(log^2 k) on HSTs, giving O(log^2 k log n) on n-point metrics
a single randomized online policy has expected cost <= C (log(k+1))^2 OPT + B against oblivious adversaries
an additive constant that 'may be enormous'
main theorem formalized: KServer.lean and UniformKServer.lean, standard axioms
